chapter: Mandeville, Bunk Johnson and society banquets
title: First hearing Bunk, and society anniversary banquets
summary: George recalls hearing Bunk in his twenties around New Orleans halls and describes how benevolent societies held banquets with food, beer and a band.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Just checking on. Oh, when was the first time you ever heard Bunk to your knowledge?

Well, the first time I heard Bunk was in his twenties. That's the first time I heard Bunk when Bunk was a younger man. I heard Bunk in New Orleans too. I heard Bunk here on Parades. I heard Bunk at Banquets. You know, we called Bunk kids. We called them Bunk kids at the Hopes Hall. I heard him at the – they never gave too many at the Economy Hall. But the Perseverance Hall and the New Hall there and also the – where the big I-Lewy used to stay at Artesian Hall. That's where the Bunk was mostly.

Tell a little bit more about those Bunk kids. They had one at the Union when you were up in Chicago the last time. Dick and I were invited over. But of course there they lined up, you know, and went around and got chicken. It wasn't served to them or anything. But were the old Bunk kids more formal? How did they – what did they do? Have music or what all did they do?

Well, I'll tell you how they did. The organizations would have, say like it would be the anniversary of the society. It would be two years old probably next – this year or three or whatever year, you know – well every year on that date they would have this banquet. Well they'd take – so many members would be of the Catholic faiths, so many would be of the Baptist faiths. But one year they'd go to a Baptist church if it was a Baptist, well they'd go on a Sunday evening, you know, for this service. If it was a Catholic they'd go for Mass in the morning of the day of the banquet. And all the members would get in the line and walk. No music though. We'd meet at the church and they'd walk and they'd come to the hall and they'd have the chocolate and the ham and donuts. And then at a certain time of the day around 12 they'd have the dinner. And at one o'clock the music would start until six. Four, five?
Six. Under six. And then each member would have an invitation. I'd give you an invitation. Sometimes some fellows could get in without invitations, sometimes they couldn't.
Did they have any speeches or other kind of entertainments or after-dinner speeches or dancing later?

No, dancing after the dinner which would be at 12 o'clock. And then the band would start at one. Around about 2, 2.30 and they'd call the band down. Everything was free. They'd feed the band. Yeah, everything was free.

Beer with no bottle beer. It was all cake beer. They'd have big agate pitches. They'd serve it in a lot of pitches. And everybody would have a good time. If it was a children organization, well they'd have beer for the grown people and ice cream and cake for the children and lemonade, you know. They'd have a really, really good time. A lot of times there'd be a lot of fuss about this member went and said he didn't get enough for the money. You know, each member would be taxed so much, but they didn't get enough to eat for their money. They said the committees would take it all and all such things as that. Back to Bunk for a minute.
